title: CSC 2400 Module 11 Part 2: The 0/1 Knapsack Problem (Dynamic Programming)

questions.q: In the 0/1 knapsack problem, what does the capacity C limit?
choices: The total size of the chosen items
The total value of the chosen items
The number of items that may be chosen
The value of the single most valuable item
questions.explain: The constraint is sum of s_i over the chosen set S ≤ C. Value is what we maximize; size is what the capacity limits.

questions.q: An optimal 0/1 knapsack solution must use exactly C units of capacity.
questions.explain: The constraint is ≤ C, not = C. In the worked example (C = 6) the optimum {3, 4} uses only 5 units for value 8, while the exact fill {1, 3} is worth only 7.

questions.q: What does the "0/1" in 0/1 knapsack mean?
choices: Each item is either taken once or not taken at all
Each item may be taken as any fraction from 0 to 1
Every item has a value of either 0 or 1
The knapsack is either completely empty or completely full
questions.explain: Each item is taken exactly once (1) or not at all (0). No fractions of an item and no extra copies.

questions.q: Because values are nonnegative and the empty set is always feasible, the optimal knapsack value is never negative.
questions.explain: The empty set has total size 0 ≤ C and value 0, so the optimum is at least 0.

questions.q: Checking every possible subset of n items by brute force examines how many subsets?
questions.explain: Each item is in or out, so there are 2^n subsets (16 for the 4-item worked example). That is exponential, which DP avoids by reusing answers to overlapping subproblems.

questions.q: Which of these are assumptions of the knapsack formulation in this lesson?
choices: The capacity C is a nonnegative integer
Each item's value is at least its size
Items are listed in order of decreasing value
questions.explain: The input has nonnegative values, positive integer sizes and a nonnegative integer capacity. Integer sizes and capacity let the DP make one column per capacity 0..C. Nothing relates value to size, and the items can come in any order.

questions.q: What does A[i][c] represent?
choices: Max value using only items 1..i with total size at most c
Max value using items i..n with total size exactly c
Min total size needed to reach value c using items 1..i
The value of item i when the remaining capacity is c
questions.explain: A[i][c] is the maximum value obtainable using only items 1 through i with capacity at most c. The index i is an item prefix and c is a capacity limit.

questions.q: If item i does not fit (s_i > c), what is A[i][c]?
questions.explain: An item that is too large must be excluded, so the best value is the best using items 1..i-1 with the same capacity: A[i][c] = A[i-1][c].

questions.q: When item i fits (s_i ≤ c), which expression is the "include item i" option?
questions.explain: Including item i adds its value v_i, uses up its size s_i, and fills the leftover capacity c - s_i from items 1..i-1 only (row i-1), because item i is already used.

questions.q: The base case A[i][0] = 0 for every i depends on the assumption that every item size is positive.
questions.explain: With positive sizes nothing fits in capacity 0, so only the empty set is feasible. A size-0 item with positive value would fit in capacity 0 and make A[i][0] positive.

questions.q: Maximum-weight independent set on a path needs only one index per subproblem (a prefix). Why does knapsack also need a capacity index?
choices: Including an item leaves a subproblem with less room
Items must be sorted by size before the table is filled
The capacity determines how many items are available
Each item's value changes as the capacity changes
questions.explain: In the include case the leftover problem has a different capacity, c - s_i. A subproblem described only by "items 1..i" cannot record how much room is left, so the table is two-dimensional.

questions.q: The property that an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems is called what?
questions.explain: Optimal substructure: an optimal knapsack solution either excludes the last item (reducing to fewer items, same capacity) or includes it (reducing to fewer items, capacity C - s_n).

questions.q: Which table entry holds the answer to the original problem with n items and capacity C?
questions.explain: A[n][C] is the best value using all n items with capacity at most C, which is the original problem. A[0][C] and A[n][0] are base cases equal to 0.

questions.q: Worked example: C = 6; item 1 (value 3, size 4), item 2 (value 2, size 3), item 3 (value 4, size 2), item 4 (value 4, size 3). Given A[2][5] = 3 and A[2][3] = 2, compute A[3][5].
questions.explain: Item 3 (s = 2) fits: max(A[2][5], 4 + A[2][3]) = max(3, 4 + 2) = 6. This is items 2 and 3.

questions.q: Worked example: C = 6; item 1 (value 3, size 4), item 2 (value 2, size 3), item 3 (value 4, size 2), item 4 (value 4, size 3). Compute A[2][4].
questions.explain: Row 1 is 0,0,0,0,3,3,3. Item 2 (s = 3) fits at c = 4: max(A[1][4], 2 + A[1][1]) = max(3, 2 + 0) = 3. Excluding item 2 wins.

questions.q: Worked example: C = 6; item 1 (value 3, size 4), item 2 (value 2, size 3), item 3 (value 4, size 2), item 4 (value 4, size 3). Row 3 of the table is 0, 0, 4, 4, 4, 6, 7 for c = 0..6. Compute A[4][5].
questions.explain: Item 4 (s = 3) fits: max(A[3][5], 4 + A[3][2]) = max(6, 4 + 4) = 8. This is items 3 and 4.

questions.q: Item i has value 5 and size 2. You know A[i-1][6] = 9 and A[i-1][4] = 3. What is A[i][6]?
questions.explain: max(A[i-1][6], 5 + A[i-1][6 - 2]) = max(9, 5 + 3) = max(9, 8) = 9. Excluding item i is better here.

questions.q: C = 5; item 1 (value 4, size 1), item 2 (value 5, size 2), item 3 (value 7, size 3). Fill the table and give A[3][5].
When item i fits, the cell A[i][c] is computed from which two cells?
questions.explain: It reads the cell directly above, (i-1, c), and the cell one row up and s_i columns to the left, (i-1, c - s_i). Both are in the previous row.

questions.q: In the full 2-D table, sweeping the capacities within a row from C down to 0 (instead of 0 up to C) would change the computed values.
questions.explain: Every cell in row i depends only on row i-1, which is already complete, so the sweep order within a row does not matter in the 2-D table. Order only matters in the 1-D version.

questions.q: While reconstructing the chosen items at cell (i, c), you find A[i][c] ≠ A[i-1][c]. What do you do?
choices: Take item i and set c to c - s_i
Skip item i and leave c unchanged
Take item i and leave c unchanged
Skip item i and set c to c - s_i
questions.explain: If the exclude value A[i-1][c] does not equal A[i][c], the include option produced the maximum, so item i was taken and its size is removed from the remaining capacity. Then move to row i-1.

questions.q: On a tie (A[i][c] = A[i-1][c] even though including item i would also reach that value), excluding item i still leads to an optimal selection.
questions.explain: A[i-1][c] already achieves the optimal value, so excluding is always safe. The standard rule excludes on ties.

questions.q: Worked example: C = 6; items (value, size) = (3, 4), (2, 3), (4, 2), (4, 3). Reconstruction starts at A[4][6] = 8 and takes item 4. Which cell is examined next?
questions.explain: Taking item 4 moves to row 3 and reduces capacity by s_4 = 3, from 6 to 3. A[3][3] = 4 ≠ A[2][3] = 2, so item 3 is taken next, giving {3, 4}.

questions.q: C = 5; item 1 (value 4, size 1), item 2 (value 5, size 2), item 3 (value 7, size 3). The table rows for c = 0..5 are row 1: 0,4,4,4,4,4; row 2: 0,4,5,9,9,9; row 3: 0,4,5,9,11,12. Which items does the standard backward reconstruction select?
C = 4; item 1 (value 5, size 4) and item 2 (value 5, size 4). The table gives A[1][4] = 5 and A[2][4] = 5. Using the rule that excludes on ties, which items are selected?
questions.explain: A[2][4] = A[1][4] = 5 is a tie, so item 2 is skipped and c stays 4. A[1][4] = 5 ≠ A[0][4] = 0, so item 1 is taken. Both items together have size 8, which does not fit.

questions.q: Once the full table is filled, how long does reconstructing the chosen items take?
questions.explain: The backward walk does one comparison per item (rows n down to 1), so it is O(n). It needs the full 2-D table because it compares each row with the row before it.

questions.q: There are n = 30 items and capacity C = 99. How many entries does the full DP table have?
questions.explain: The table has (n + 1) rows and (C + 1) columns: 31 × 100 = 3,100 entries.

questions.q: What are the time and space costs of the full 2-D knapsack DP?
questions.explain: There are (n + 1)(C + 1) = O(nC) subproblems with O(1) work each, plus O(n) reconstruction, for O(nC) time. Storing the full table takes O(nC) space.

questions.q: The O(nC) knapsack DP runs in time polynomial in the length of its input (the number of bits needed to write the input).
questions.explain: C takes only O(log C) bits to write, but the work grows with the numeric value of C. If C has b bits, C can be about 2^b, so the algorithm is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial in input length.

questions.q: Why is the O(nC) knapsack algorithm called pseudo-polynomial?
choices: Work grows with C's numeric value, which can be exponential in its bit length
It is polynomial only after the items are sorted by value-to-size ratio
It is polynomial on average but exponential on worst-case inputs
It needs polynomial time but an exponential amount of memory
questions.explain: O(nC) is polynomial in n and in the magnitude of C, but C needs only about log2 C bits, so the running time can be exponential in the input's bit length.

questions.q: If the capacity C is written with b bits, the O(nC) running time is, in the worst case:
questions.explain: A b-bit number can be as large as about 2^b, so O(nC) = O(n · 2^b), which is exponential in the bit length of C.

questions.q: With n fixed, the capacity grows from C = 255 (8 bits) to C = 65,535 (16 bits). By what factor does the number of DP table columns grow?
questions.explain: Columns go from C + 1 = 256 to 65,536, a factor of 256, while the capacity's written length only doubles from 8 to 16 bits. This is why the runtime is pseudo-polynomial.

questions.q: Using total work ≈ (number of subproblems) × (work per subproblem) + reconstruction, how much work does the knapsack DP do per subproblem?
questions.explain: Each cell needs at most one addition and one comparison, so O(1). With O(nC) cells and O(n) reconstruction, the total is O(nC).

questions.q: In the O(C)-space 1-D version of 0/1 knapsack, how should c be looped for each item i?
questions.explain: Capacities must be processed in decreasing order so that dp[c - s_i] still holds the value from before item i was considered, and item i cannot be used twice.

questions.q: One item with value 5 and size 3, C = 9. A 1-D array starting at all zeros is updated with c going UP from 3 to 9 using dp[c] = max(dp[c], 5 + dp[c - 3]). What is dp[9] at the end?
questions.explain: Going up: dp[3] = 5, dp[6] = 5 + dp[3] = 10, dp[9] = 5 + dp[6] = 15, which counts the item three times. That is unbounded behavior; the correct 0/1 answer (looping down) is 5.

questions.q: The 1-D version finds the optimal value in O(C) space, but the standard backward walk cannot recover the chosen items from it.
questions.explain: The 1-D array overwrites earlier rows, so A[i][c] can no longer be compared with A[i-1][c]. Use the full table if you need the selected items.

questions.q: A student uses A[i][c] = max(A[i-1][c], v_i + A[i][c - s_i]). Which problem does this actually solve?
choices: Knapsack that must be filled exactly
questions.explain: Reading the current row i in the include case lets A[i][c - s_i] already contain item i, so the item can be counted more than once. For 0/1 knapsack the include term must read row i-1.

questions.q: Why does looping c downward make the 1-D array correct for 0/1 knapsack?
choices: dp[c - s_i] still holds its row i-1 value when read
Larger capacities never read smaller capacities
It processes the items in decreasing order of size
It forces each capacity to be filled exactly
questions.explain: Going from high c to low c, the smaller index c - s_i has not been overwritten yet in this pass, so it still reflects items 1..i-1 only and item i is used at most once.

questions.q: In the 1-D loop for c from C down to s_i, what happens to dp[c] for capacities c < s_i during item i's pass?
questions.explain: Item i does not fit at those capacities, so the loop skips them and they keep their previous value, which is exactly the exclude value A[i-1][c].

questions.q: C = 10; item X (value 7, size 6), item Y (value 5, size 5), item Z (value 5, size 5). Greedy by highest value-to-size ratio takes items in ratio order whenever they still fit. What total value does it get?
questions.explain: X has the best ratio (about 1.17), so greedy takes X and has 4 units left; Y and Z (size 5) no longer fit, total 7. The optimal choice is {Y, Z}: size 10, value 10.

questions.q: C = 6; item A (value 9, size 5), item B (value 6, size 3), item C (value 6, size 3). Greedy by largest value takes A and gets 9. What is the optimal value?
questions.explain: After A only 1 unit remains, so greedy stops at 9. Taking B and C uses size 6 for value 12. A with B or C has size 8, which is too big.

questions.q: Choosing items by greatest value-to-size ratio always gives an optimal 0/1 knapsack solution.
questions.explain: Items cannot be split, so a high-ratio item can leave awkward unused space. Example: C = 4 with items (v 5, s 3), (v 3, s 2), (v 3, s 2). Ratio greedy gets 5, but the two small items give 6.

questions.q: For the case where item i fits, a student writes the include option as s_i + A[i-1][c - v_i]. What is wrong?
choices: It reads the current row, so items repeat
It should read row i+1 instead of row i-1
Nothing; it equals the correct include term
questions.explain: The size is subtracted from the capacity index (c - s_i) and the value is added to the result (v_i + ...). The correct term is v_i + A[i-1][c - s_i].

questions.q: Which of these are mistakes when solving 0/1 knapsack with DP?
choices: Reading A[i][c - s_i] in the include case
Requiring the total size to equal C exactly
Subtracting the item's size from the capacity index
Calling the O(nC) algorithm polynomial in input length
Copying A[i-1][c] when item i is larger than c
questions.explain: Reading row i allows reuse (unbounded knapsack), the constraint is ≤ C rather than = C, and O(nC) is pseudo-polynomial. Subtracting s_i from c and copying A[i-1][c] when the item does not fit are both correct.

questions.q: In the C++ implementation, DP row i corresponds to item i (1-based). Where is item i's size stored?
questions.explain: C++ vectors are 0-indexed, so item i's data is at values[i - 1] and sizes[i - 1]. Forgetting the - 1 is an off-by-one bug.

questions.q: The table is declared as vector<vector<int>> dp(n + 1, vector<int>(capacity + 1, 0)). Why does it have n + 1 rows?
choices: Row 0 is the no-items base case
The extra row holds each item's size
C++ vectors cannot have exactly n rows
questions.explain: Rows 0..n: row 0 means no items are available and is all zeros (the base case A[0][c] = 0), which the zero initialization already sets. Likewise capacity + 1 columns cover c = 0..C.

questions.q: The C++ loop first sets dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c], then, only if the item fits, replaces it with the include value when that is larger. This computes the same values as the two-case recurrence.
questions.explain: Starting from the exclude value and taking the max with the include value only when sizes[i - 1] ≤ c is exactly the two cases: copy when the item does not fit, max of exclude and include when it does.

questions.q: Why does the program call reverse on the selected vector before printing it?
choices: The walk finds items from n down to 1
The DP table was filled from row n to row 0
Items must be printed by decreasing value
reverse removes the items that were tied
questions.explain: Reconstruction walks i from n down to 1, so items are collected last to first. Reversing prints them in increasing item order.

questions.q: The program is run with n = 3, capacity 4, and items (value, size): item 1 (5, 3), item 2 (4, 2), item 3 (3, 2). What does it print after "Selected item numbers:"? (Give the item numbers separated by spaces.)
questions.explain: Rows for c = 0..4: row 1: 0,0,0,5,5; row 2: 0,0,4,5,5; row 3: 0,0,4,5,7. A[3][4] = 7 ≠ 5: take item 3, c = 2. A[2][2] = 4 ≠ 0: take item 2, c = 0. Skip item 1. After reverse it prints "2 3" (maximum value 7).
